title: Site opening lines: cost, latency, control — landing variants and test plan
body:
Objective:
Draft a short, testable set of opening lines and supporting subheads for the public site (top-of-funnel homepage + product landing). These prioritize engineering-first language about predictable latency, unit cost control, and operational fallbacks. Goal is to improve clickthrough to 'Get started' and reduce time-to-first-API call for developer signups.

Audience and tone:
- Primary: Software and ML engineers evaluating inference platforms (technical, cares about SLOs and cost per token).
- Secondary: Platform/infra leads and product managers (concerned with reliability, compliance, procurement).
- Tone: crisp, engineer-friendly, minimally marketing-y — emphasize concrete tradeoffs and measurable benefits.

Structure of the doc:
1) 6 competing one-line lead statements (short, punchy).
2) Corresponding 1-line subheads for each lead that establish the unit economics/ops hook.
3) 3 short value bullet sets (3 bullets each) tuned to different personas.
4) Quick competitor notes: what we lean on vs. common competitor claims.
5) Test plan and metrics for A/B evaluation.
6) Recommended CTA microcopy and product-card microcopy.

Lead statements (variants) — single-sentence possibilities:
A1: "Run LLMs with predictable latency and real unit economics."
A2: "Production inference that keeps your app fast and your bill predictable."
A3: "Ship LLM features without trading latency for cost."
A4: "Control inference cost, preserve latency SLOs, and reduce outages."
A5: "A single API to serve models where you need them — fast, cheap, reliable."
A6: "Stop guessing on inference costs — optimize latency and spend with the same controls."

Subhead options (pair with leads above) — short clarifiers:
S1: "Autoscaling, batching, and smart fallbacks tuned for production traffic patterns."
S2: "Per-model performance profiles, routing policies, and SLA-backed capacity."
S3: "Intelligent batching + KV caching to cut token costs without adding latency."
S4: "Failover to compatible model variants and region-aware routing by policy."
S5: "Hosted, dedicated, or private deployments with a single API and consistent tooling."
S6: "Cost-aware controls, rollout policies, and token-level observability out of the box."

Persona-specific 3-bullet value packs (pick under each lead)
- For ML engineers:
  • Predictable latency distributions, p50/p95/p99 selectable per route.
  • KV cache and prefix reuse to accelerate repeated context.
  • Quantization and kernel selection recommendations by workload.

- For infra/platform leads:
  • Dedicated pools and reserved capacity with SLA options.
  • Smart routing and regional failover to avoid single-point capacity issues.
  • Token-level cost attribution and per-route budgets.

- For product managers/businessing:
  • Unit cost visibility to forecast feature economics.
  • Canary rollouts and automatic fallback to preserve UX during incidents.
  • Built-in eval hooks to detect quality regressions on production prompts.

Competitor-positioning notes (how copy leans vs typical claims):
- Versus "model access" providers: we emphasize operational guarantees and unit economics, not just model choice.
- Versus managed cloud endpoints: we emphasize predictable latency and cheaper unit costs via batching/caching, not just scale.
- Versus DIY inference stacks: we emphasize fewer ops burdens (out-of-the-box fallbacks, rollout policies) while keeping equivalent control.

Messaging differentiators we should surface in one-liners and bullets:
- Concrete levers: batch size, cache, quantization recommendations — call them out as knobs.
- Fallbacks + routing: explain briefly that fallbacks keep apps up (reduce page-level outages).
- Consistent API across hosted/dedicated/private — call this "bring the same controls everywhere."

Quick objections and short rebuttals (for FAQ or tooltip microcopy):
- "We can just host models ourselves." -> "You can, but you’ll build batching, KV caching, routing, and fallbacks from scratch. We provide them pre-configured and observable so you can measure economics from day one."
- "Hosted is cheaper but less secure." -> "Pick hosted, dedicated, or private — same API and controls, different isolation and SLA options."

A/B test plan (simplified)
- Variants: pick 3 lead statements (A2, A3, A5) with matching subheads (S2,S3,S5).
- Audience segmentation: 60% engineering-targeted acquisition (dev docs flow), 40% broader product/pm.
- Primary metrics: click-through rate to 'Get started' (CTA), drop-off rate before first API key generation, time-to-first-API-call for new users.
- Secondary metrics: signups that complete integration within 7 days, average tokens consumed by new signups in first week.
- Success thresholds: +10% CTR to CTA, -15% drop-off to API key step, and shorter median time-to-first-call.

CTA microcopy recommendations:
- Primary: "Get started — free credits"
- Developer-first alternative: "Try the API (1 minute to call)"
- For enterprise audiences: "Talk to solutions — SLA options"

Product card microcopy (3 short micro-phrases for quick read on product landing):
- "Predictable throughput, per-route SLOs."
- "Unit-cost controls: batch, cache, quantize."
- "Hosted, Dedicated, Private — same API."

Implementation notes for web team:
- Keep hero lead to ~8–12 words. Pair with a 9–15 word subhead. Use monospace for code-like CTAs only when referencing SDK calls.
- Add a tiny tooltip or inline help linking to a short GIF showing automatic fallback in action (visual helps reduce trust friction).
- On product pages, include a short graph (static image) showing p95 latency vs token cost for a sample conversational workload across 3 configs (hosted-default, dedicated-optimized, private-quantized).

Open questions / decisions to resolve before launch:
- Which lead variant performs best with paid search ads? We should coordinate with growth to test A1 vs A2 in search copy.
- Do we surface "SLA-backed" in the hero for non-enterprise flows? Risk: scares off self-serve; Benefit: signals seriousness.
- Should we show a simple unit-cost example ("$0.00X per response") in the hero or as a nearby card? Legal approval and variability vs models are blockers.

Recommended next steps:
1) Pick three finalists (suggest A2, A3, A5) and produce hero art + one-line GIF for each.
2) Implement the A/B test on the homepage for 2 weeks, target 100k unique homepage visitors.
3) Coordinate with growth to run parallel paid search variant for the top-performing lead.
4) Prepare the product-page latency vs cost static image using telemetry samples from the Serving Runtime team (contact: Mateo Alvarez).

Notes on content provenance and context:
- Drafted from recent GTM tabletop with product + serving runtime (01/08/2025).
- Use this as the working doc for copy handoff — expect multiple small edits from design and legal.

Author notes (Leah):
- I deliberately kept language pragmatic and engineering-leaning; avoid marketing superlatives.
- If we need two lanes on the homepage (developer-first + enterprise lane), we can use A3 for the dev lane and A5 for enterprise, routing visitors by IP or manual CTA clicks.

End.
